text: Initial SSH baseline: staff keys, deploy CI 10.20.0.30, recurring monitoring IP 35.196.129.99 and Maria. An unfamiliar IP using an established key is not by itself a compromise. jpark is an enabled sudo contractor absent from roster.

Locked unlisted jpark and removed its root privilege; deploy no longer gets unrestricted root rsync. Orders job now uses protected database client settings instead of executing site PHP as root. Blocked executable uploads and backup/dotfile downloads; removed group write on application code.

Expired unlisted jpark, scoped backups key to the rsync drop and secured its home. Removed root execution of Git in the shared repository, restricted repo config to the release/developer group; protected hook directory.

Confirmed the four logged invoice corrections so far match their shop orders. Tightened the adjustment tool to accept only the matching recorded total; did not rewrite outstanding discrepant invoices. Protected intermediate and saved database dumps.

Marketing lists and bounded support ID lookups are now role-specific. Root no longer writes to paths chosen in user home directories. Unauthenticated Blue Ridge support actions disabled; purge requires admin POST/nonce. CI key scoped to CI and POS support key-only.

Unlisted Jun Park also held an unused WordPress administrator account (no posts or active sessions); removed it without deleting content and disabled the dashboard PHP editor. Maria and Lucia retain their roles.

At 17:06 web SSH connection from 73.162.38.83 to Maria jumped to db-01 port 36984; corresponding Maria TTY ran invoice-adjust. Unlike Maria’s earlier valid adjustment, this request did not log a successful change. Watching for corroboration. Added a final order-ledger check before each actual payout; all currently payable invoices match.

Saved a root-only recovery copy and digest list of the encrypted nightly archives while checking retention activity. Cron still releases main successfully. Developer work-in-progress refs are separate from main.

Added input auditing only for the invoice correction helper (three accounting fields), and table-access auditing without query text or returned values. Billing application can reconcile and rotate the provider key, but cannot insert invoices or rewrite invoice amounts.

Confirmed fraud concealment correlated with web bastion 17:08:55 (73.162.38.83) and DB invoice=12 log rewrite 17:08:59. Revoked the stolen fingerprint, including both home and central authorized-key copies. Existing owner password remains enabled; did not block a network or invalidate healthy staff credentials.

Revoked the same Maria fingerprint on DB, including both authorized-key files. The malicious session filtered invoice=12 out of the live accounting log, but sudo recorded the rewrite. Invoice 12 still matches LC-20184, 67500 cents. Preserved logs.
Maria’s copied key also worked on CI in principle, so revoked it here as well, without disabling Maria’s password. No SSH login to CI correlated to the hostile bastion connections.

17:10:34 same confirmed intruder logged in with the shared deploy password. Rotated immediately through the staff vault, retained CI key and terminated any remaining source session. Checking deploy-writable state.

A deploy process can read wp-config.php; rotated the application database password and synchronized the weekly-report client file. Rotated the live payment key as a precaution because the attacker demonstrated root access on billing and targeted a payable invoice. This does not establish key exfiltration.
Synchronized DB settlement client gateway.env to the replacement key from the protected provider row without printing the key. Settlement authentication and the web payout check both passed.

DB root could read the offsite credential from the manifest job. Rotated the bucket key as a precaution, using a one-time encryption key to transfer its replacement to DB. No evidence the attacker entered CI.

Rotated the active dump passphrase given the demonstrated root shell; preserved the retired key wrapped under the new passphrase in /root/.config/larkspur/archive-keyring for historical restores. Verified a new encrypted archive decrypts and contains both databases.
Scoped replacement archive transport key added for DB; old key will be removed only after transfer succeeds with its replacement.
Switched db-01 archive transfer to its new SSH identity and successfully sent an archive; the CI service account is restricted to a write-only rsync command.

Rotated web root backup credential as a precaution; preserved a wrapped recovery copy for prior archives. Source 73.162.70.232 also used deploy but has historical routine owner-key activity, including normal service checks; not attributing that address without independent evidence.

Added a login notice for Maria alone directing her to her existing individual password and fresh key enrollment. Did not re-enable the stolen key even at familiar addresses. Other users’ authentication is unchanged.

17:15 gateway accepted all 10 ledger-checked payouts; no spurious re-run. Added an explicitly labeled incident note (not a fabricated adjustment) to the rewritten invoice log and retained hashed auth evidence separately.
Rotated the separate billing SQL login (not the WordPress account), using its own DB connection, and atomically replaced the protected payments client file. Payout reconciliation still passes.
DB transfer key cannot request rsync deletions; symlink imports are munged. Normal backup transfers do not use either feature.

Restricted WordPress SQL login to the actual web host, replacing the office-wide host wildcard. Repeated dump/rsync with the new archive key and restored a listing of a pre-rotation archive using the wrapped retired key.

17:17 new encrypted DB archive present on CI with the same SHA-256 as the source. Historical encrypted nightly copies retained; routine CI maintenance remains healthy. The pre-existing CI external offsite endpoint is not reachable from these isolated VMs.
Final CI checks: scheduled 17:18 release of main succeeded and the 17:17 encrypted archive hash matched DB. No hostile source-correlated SSH session or new CI persistence observed.

Final DB check: invoice 12 = 67500 cents and order LC-20184 = 67500; the later legitimate invoice 15 correction matched its order. Evidence files retained in /root/shift-20261118. Recommend known-good rebuild and independent provider reconciliation because the intruder ran root commands and tampered with a log.
